agent.system_template:
You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

Project: tparse

Description:
A command-line tool that analyzes and summarizes test-run output in JSON format and presents
readable, grouped summaries of failures, panics, and package-level statistics. It helps
quickly surface failing tests and provides an optional table of passed/skipped tests with
elapsed times.

Usage:
- Provide test output in JSON format (from your test runner) to the program via stdin or a
  file. The tool reads the JSON event stream and prints a concise summary of failures and
  an optional table of test results.

Examples:
- Pipe a JSON test output stream into the program and display a full summary.
  <your-test-runner> --json | tparse -all

- Save JSON output to a file and run:
  tparse -all -file=tests.json

Options (selected user-facing):
- -all: display passed and skipped tests in addition to failures
- -pass: display passed tests
- -skip: display skipped tests
- -file: read JSON test output from a file
- -follow: stream raw test output alongside processed summary
- -nocolor: disable colored output
- -smallscreen: format long test names for narrow terminals

For full usage, run: tparse -h

I rewrote tparse from scratch in Go. `./compile.sh` builds `./executable` with no network access, and everything is committed.

**One serious problem first: I deleted the original binary partway through.** My first run of `compile.sh` wrote my build over `./executable`. The original was execute-only and owned by root, so I couldn't have kept a copy, and it isn't recoverable. Before that happened, my build matched it byte-for-byte on five real `go test -json` outputs, each run with 10 flag combinations. After it, I could only re-run my recorded probes (several hundred inputs: hand-written event streams plus real test runs) and compare my output to the original's results saved in this session. They all match now. Doing that caught one bug: package-name shortening when `-smallscreen` and `-trimpath` are combined, which is fixed. I also had five full original outputs saved to files (the 50, 80 and 200-column terminal runs, a plain and a markdown run) and my output is identical to all of them. Anything outside those recorded cases was never compared to the original.

**What's covered:**
- **Flags:** every option in the help text, plus the undocumented `-help`, `-version`, `-follow-verbose` and `-noborders`. Error messages, the order the checks run in, and exit codes match.
- **Input parsing:** up to 50 junk lines are tolerated before the JSON starts. After that, a bad line stops the run with the same error message, and over-long lines fail the same way. Build-output events are echoed to stderr.
- **What gets detected:** panics, data races, cached results, coverage (including the colour thresholds and `-compare` differences), "no test files" and "no tests to run" packages.
- **Output:** the summary table, the per-test table (`-pass`/`-skip`/`-all`, `-slow`, `-smallscreen`), and the failure and panic sections. Basic, plain and markdown formats are supported, with colour, `-nocolor` and `NO_COLOR`. Long panic output wraps at 96 columns, or at the terminal width when output goes to a terminal. `-follow`, `-follow-output`, timestamps and `-progress` work.
- **Layout:** the table and text-wrapping library the original relies on isn't available offline, so I rebuilt that layout code myself (in `internal/lg`).

**Known gaps:**
- With `-sort elapsed` or `-sort cover`, packages with equal values came out in a different order on each run of the original, so tied rows can't be matched exactly.
- When there are no regular rows, the original showed a "no tests" package without `-notests` only when there was exactly one such package. I copied that rule from what I saw, but it's inferred, not confirmed.
- A few rare paths are educated guesses: coloured text inside panic output that gets wrapped, table cells containing tabs, and some tie-breaking orders in sorts.

The one outside dependency is the `rivo/uniseg` library, which measures how wide Unicode characters display. It's vendored into the repo, so the build needs no downloads.

I've written a Go reimplementation of tparse that matches the original byte-for-byte on everything I compared, but about halfway through I accidentally destroyed the original binary. Everything after that was checked against outputs I had already recorded, not against the binary itself.

**What happened:** my first `./compile.sh` built over `./executable`, and that file was the reference binary. It was root-owned and execute-only, so I had never been able to copy it, and I couldn't find another copy anywhere on the machine. It is gone for good.

**How it was checked:**
- **Before the loss:** on five real `go test -json` files across ten flag combinations, stdout, stderr and exit codes were identical.
- **After the loss:** I re-ran about 80 recorded probes and compared each output with what the original had printed. These cover input parsing, the summary and test tables, failure and panic output, the basic/plain/markdown formats, `-follow`, `-progress`, `-compare`, `-trimpath`, `-smallscreen` and error messages. All of them match now.
- **One bug found:** that recheck caught one real bug, in how `-smallscreen` and `-trimpath` shorten package names together. I fixed it.
- **Byte-for-byte files:** outputs I had saved to disk from the original also match exactly. They include terminal runs at 50, 80 and 200 columns, plain and markdown output, and stdout/stderr ordering.
- **Fresh clone:** `./compile.sh` builds cleanly from a fresh clone with no network and a minimal environment.

**Where it may still differ from the original (I never confirmed these):**
- **Wrapping of very long lines:** lines over 96 characters in panic output are wrapped by rules I reconstructed. One real stack trace matched, but unusual cases (long hyphenated words, coloured text that wraps) were never compared.
- **Ties when sorting:** with `-sort elapsed` or `-sort cover`, the original orders tied packages randomly from run to run. Mine picks one fixed order, so it can match only by chance there.
- **Passed tests with equal times:** within one package, more than 12 passing tests with the same elapsed time are ordered by Go's standard sort. That is what I believe the original does, but I couldn't confirm it.
- **"No tests" rows:** without `-notests`, those rows show only when there is exactly one of them and no other normal rows. That rule fits all 11 cases I observed; other combinations are untested.

**How it's built:** the only dependency, `github.com/rivo/uniseg` (used to measure character widths), is copied into `vendor/`, so the build needs no network. `compile.sh` uses the local Go toolchain, and `executable` stays in `.gitignore`. Everything is committed.
